meta.value_key: Feature -> values use the Dirr tag-matrix column names (e.g. 'Acute (base)', 'Pinnate (venation)') because they are the assertion keys; display labels are in the feature metadata.

values.definition: compounded with the leaflets or segments along each side of a common axis or rachis; feather-like.
A compound leaf arrangement in which all leaflets radiate from a single common point, like fan blades, rather than from a central axis, like a feather
Woody plant with a single central axis, branching 6 feet or more from the ground.
Woody plant with several stems branching from or near the ground.
Twining, clasping, or self-clinging growth habit.
Low-growing, spreading or mat-forming woody or semi-woody plant; spreads by stolons, rhizomes, or rooting stems rather than growing upright.
An unbranched inflorescence with flowers attached to the central axis on individual stalks.
A branched inflorescence with repeated branching from the main axis, often composed of smaller racemes, spikes, or corymbs.
A flat-topped or convex inflorescence in which the main axis ends in a flower, with branches arising from below. Outer flowers open last.
A flat-topped inflorescence in which flower stalks attach at different levels along the main axis but reach approximately the same height.
A slim, cylindrical cluster of small flowers that typically hang from tree branches; flowers are unisexual (male or female) and wind-pollinated.
An inflorescence in which all flower stalks radiate from a single point at the top of the main stem, like the spokes of an umbrella.
A dense, compact inflorescence of many small flowers crowded together on a short axis.
A single flower, not grouped with others.
An unbranched inflorescence with flowers attached directly to the elongated central axis, without individual stalks.
A spike-like inflorescence with small flowers crowded on a fleshy central axis, typically partially enclosed by a spathe, a large petal-like leaf surrounding the spike.
Leaves and buds directly across from each other on the stem, two per node.
Leaves and buds staggered along the stem, one per node, never directly across from each other.
Three or more leaves radiating from a single node, encircling the stem.
Leaves and buds paired close together on the stem but not at exactly the same level, neither opposite nor fully alternatating.
having an apex whose sides are gradually concave and tapering to a point.
with a shallow notch at the apex.
abruptly terminated by a mucro.
with an apex somewhat abruptly and concavely constricted into an elongated sharp-pointed tip.
the apex being cordate.
rounded, approaching the semi-circular.
having an apex whose sides are straight and taper to a point.
as if cut off at right angles to the primary axis; a term applicable to bases or apices.
wedge-shaped with essentially straight side, the structure attached at the narrow end.
heart-shaped, with a sinus and rounded lobes; properly a term applied only to bases of leaves and bracts, but frequently employed to designate a structure of ovate outline and heart-shaped base.
having the shape of an arrow-head and the basal lobes pointed outwards at or nearly at right angles to the mid-rib.
lop-sided, as one side of a leaf base larger, wider or more rounded than the other.
shaped like an arrow-head with the basal lobes pointing directly downward (backward) or inward.
bearing ear-like appendages, as the projections of some leaf and petal bases.
having an apex whose sides are straight and taper to a point.
A base with a smoothly curved outline, neither pointed nor flat.
as if cut off at right angles to the primary axis; a term applicable to bases or apices.
Lobes arranged symmetrically along a central midrib, each corresponding to a lateral vein. Characteristic of oaks (Quercus), alders (Alnus), and similar genera.
Lobes radiating from a central basal point, each corresponding to a primary vein from the petiole attachment. Characteristic of maples (Acer), sweetgum (Liquidambar), and similar genera.
saw-toothed, the teeth pointing forward.
Toothed margin with teeth pointing outward rather than forward, perpendicular to the leaf edge.
A margin with no teeth, lobes, or indentations; unbroken from base to tip.
A margin with shallow, rounded scallops.
A margin divided into rounded or pointed projections cut roughly halfway to the center of the leaf.
A margin with pronounced wave-like curves in the plane of the leaf.
A margin with a wavy, rippled edge curving up and down out of the plane of the leaf.
Serrate with a secondary set of smaller teeth on each larger tooth.
Rounded at the base and tapering to a pointed tip.
Rounded at the tip and tapering toward the base (the reverse or "ob" of an ovate leaf)
Narrow and elongated, widest just below the middle and tapering to a pointed tip; lance-like.
Longer than wide with nearly parallel sides, like a rectangle with rounded corners.

Broadly ovate with a cordate base giving an overall heart-like outline; as in Cercis. Dirr uses 'heart-shaped' as a plain-English descriptor for this form, distinct from the technical base term cordate.
circular or disk-shaped.
Narrow and elongated along its full length, with roughly parallel sides.
Nearly circular in outline; approaching orbicular but slightly longer or wider than a perfect circle.
Rounded and widest at the tip, tapering to a narrow base, like a spoon.
Narrow and elongated, widest just above the middle and tapering toward a "sharp" base.
Shield-shaped, with the leaf stalk attached to the underside of the blade rather than at the margin.
Broadly rounded in outline with a shallow notch at the base, kidney-shaped.
Lower surface pale or light green, noticeably lighter than the upper surface.
Lower surface whitish or nearly white in color.
Lower surface silvery in appearance.
Lower surface with a yellow-green cast.
Lower surface covered with a waxy bloom or whitish material that rubs off readily; glaucous. Example: the bloom on many sorts of grape.
Lower surface densely woolly; hairs soft and matted. Includes tomentose and felted forms.
Lower surface shaggy with soft loose hairs; not matted. Includes pilose, villous (long soft shaggy), and silky forms.
Upper surface dark green in color.
Upper surface medium green in color.
Upper surface bright green in color.
Upper surface with a bluish or blue-green cast.
Upper surface with a grayish or gray-green cast.
Upper surface with a slight metallic gloss, less reflective than glossy.
Upper surface lacking luster or sheen.
Upper surface not hairy. A glabrous surface need not be smooth — it may be bullate or rugose.
Upper surface covered with short soft hairs; a general term encompassing strigose and hispid modifier forms.
Of leathery texture; coriaceous.
Wrinkled surface; covered with wrinkles. Includes bullate (puckered/blistered) forms.
Having a waxy surface coating.
Bearing glands; includes glandular-hirsute forms where gland-tipped stiff hairs are present.
A leaf consisting of a single, undivided blade — not divided into leaflets.
A leaf composed of two or more leaflets — individual leaf-like units attached to a common stalk rather than directly to the stem.
A long, slender conifer leaf, roughly uniform in width along its length and flat or angular in cross-section.
A needle-like gymnosperm leaf tapering to a slender, stiff point; usually sharp to the touch.
Scale-like foliage overlaps like the shingles on a roof or the scales on a fish. This type of foliage is relatively soft to the touch.
A leaf venation pattern in which secondary veins branch from a single prominent central vein (midrib), giving a feather or fishbone-like appearance.
A leaf venation pattern in which several main veins of similar size radiate from the base of the leaf, fan-like.
A venation pattern in which veins run side by side along the length of the leaf from base to tip. Unusual for woody plants.
Retains leaves year-round.
Leafless for part of the year.
Holds leaves most of the year, generally into winter.
A compound leaf divided twice: the primary leaflets of a pinnate leaf are themselves further divided into secondary leaflets (pinnae), each bearing its own leaflets along a secondary rachis/axis.
A compound leaf divided three times: each pinna of a bipinnate leaf is itself further divided, its secondary leaflets becoming stalks bearing tertiary leaflets.
